title: Van Hove singularity-driven giant Nernst signal in twisted double bilayer graphene
authors: Ujjal Roy, Monosij Roy, Unmesh Ghorai, Arkaprava Mukherjee, Ravi Kumar, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Nandini Trivedi, Rajdeep Sensarma, Subroto Mukerjee, Anindya Das
abstract: Twisted graphene layers host van Hove singularities (vHSs), peaks in the electronic density of states, thought to drive exotic phases in moiré materials, but their effect on thermal transport has remained unclear. Here we show that vHSs in twisted double bilayer graphene (tDBLG) generate an unusually large Nernst signal-the transverse voltage produced by a longitudinal temperature gradient in a magnetic field. The pronounced Nernst peaks at the vHSs of the conduction and valence bands of tDBLG are tunable by an electric field with a maximum value of $\sim 40$ $μV K^{-1} T^{-1}$ at $\sim 1$ $K$, which is comparable to the best-known Nernst materials. Our theoretical calculations show that the large enhancement of the Nernst signal arises from the Lifshitz transitions around the vHSs. These findings establish the Nernst effect as a sensitive probe of Fermi-surface topology in moiré materials, and identify a universal thermoelectric signature of van Hove singularities.
summary: This work demonstrates that Van Hove singularities in twisted double bilayer graphene lead to a giant Nernst signal, which serves as a sensitive probe of the material's Fermi surface topology. The large enhancement is theoretically linked to Lifshitz transitions occurring near these density of states peaks. By combining theory and experiment, the authors establish a universal thermoelectric signature for vHSs in moiré systems.
main_problem: To investigate how Van Hove singularities (vHSs) influence thermal transport, specifically generating a large Nernst signal in moiré materials.
main_result: The authors show that vHSs in twisted double bilayer graphene generate an unusually large and tunable Nernst signal, which is attributed to Lifshitz transitions around these singularities.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of thermopower and the Nernst effect with theoretical calculations based on semiclassical Boltzmann transport equations.
model_or_system: The physical system is twisted double bilayer graphene (tDBLG), a moiré material whose electronic structure features vHSs. Theoretical analysis uses continuum theory and minimal tight-binding models to describe band dispersion and DOS.
key_observables: Nernst signal ($S_{yx}$), Seebeck coefficient ($S_{xx}$), Density of States (DOS) peaks, and the evolution of Hall density ($n_H$).
important_parameters: Twist angles ($	ext{D}1$, $	ext{D}2$), out-of-plane displacement field ($D$), magnetic field ($B$), and carrier filling fraction ($n_0$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical calculations sometimes neglect DOS inhomogeneity due to angle variation in real devices, and some models use minimal band structures that may not capture the full complexity of tDBLG.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate measurement setups, show $R_{xx}$ and $R_{xy}$ mapping vHSs via density divergence, and compare calculated vs. measured Nernst signals ($S_{yx}$) peaking sharply at the vHS locations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the physical problem (vHS effect on thermal transport) to presenting experimental evidence of large $S_{yx}$ peaks, followed by theoretical derivations linking this enhancement to Lifshitz transitions and Fermi surface topology changes.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state transport, the concept of using topological features (like vHSs) to engineer measurable quantum responses (Nernst effect) is relevant for understanding exotic electronic states in low-dimensional or engineered quantum systems.
